text.p: On the last weekend of his last campaign for the White House, President Bill Clinton on Saturday paid a nostalgic visit to his old hometown and lamented the attack strategy of Republican rival Bob Dole.

"I really don't like a lot of what's happened in politics in the last several years. I don't like the fact that especially when it gets down toward the end and people get desperate, they think the only thing to do is try to convince you their opponent is no good," he said.

Clinton did not mention Dole by name, but his comments -- in a tone more of sorrow than anger -- clearly referred to his challenger's relentless attacks on his ethics and character in the closing days of the presidential race.

"We ought to get away from this idea that we have to demonize our opponent in order to clarify our differences," Clinton said. "But don't worry about me -- every time I get down, I remember what Mark Twain said about a dog. Mark Twain said every dog ought to have a few fleas."

Clinton's visit to Arkansas -- designed to boost the chances of some Democratic congressional candidates -- signaled his confidence that he will win re-election on Tuesday even though some polls indicate the race is tightening as the contestants near the finish line.

White House political director Doug Sosnik said the narrowing was to be expected, and did not suggest Dole might pull off an upset. "We tracked last night and we haven't seen any change in the race at all," he said.
Sosnik said that the Clinton campaign's internal polls showed that independent candidate Ross Perot "has picked up a little bit of the undecideds" but that Dole's numbers "basically stayed the same."

Clinton has led Dole by double digits in most independent polls since the start of the presidential race. The Reuters/Zogby daily tracking poll had Clinton's lead down to 3.8 percent on Saturday but others had a wider margin.
"Most of the campaigns do tighten in the end. There's no reason to think that this campaign will be any different," Sosnik said.

One sign of Clinton's confidence that he will prevail on Tuesday was his decision to cancel an election-eve visit to California, where the election is likely to be decided. He will concentrate his last-minute vote-getting efforts in Ohio, Kentucky, Iowa and South Dakota instead.
Clinton began his final countdown to Election Day in Texas, a normally pro-Republican state he thinks he has a change to win.

U.S. presidential elections are actually 51 separate contests in each of the 50 states and the District of Columbia to choose stand-ins for the candidates called electors. Two hundred seventy electoral votes are needed for victory.

Addressing a large, friendly crowd at the Alamo, the shrine of Texas liberty in San Antonio, Clinton recalled his budget battle with the Republicans last year that twice shut down the government, and said: "I thought about the Alamo."
"They said, 'Oh, the president will cave. He won't be able to stand letting the government close.' We had this economy rocking along ... and they were threatening to default on our debt," he said.

"They said, 'Oh, he'll blink.' And I said, 'You know, I'd a lot rather see the American people hurt for two or three weeks or two or three months than 20 or 30 years. Shut her down, I'm not going to buy your budget.'"

Clinton, striving to become the first Democrat since Jimmy Carter in 1976 to win the 32 electoral votes at stake in Texas, was carrying on a presidential campaign tradition in visiting the state's most famous site.

The tradition reportedly began a century ago with President Benjamin Harrison, who is said to have spoken at the chapel where Jim Bowie, Davy Crockett and 187 others died after refusing to retreat in a war for Texas independence from Mexico in 1836.
